nimtza sheeretz kenaan shebbeever hayyarden lammaarav, haya miktzoa deromit mizrachit shellah etzel edom:

Venasav lachem haggevul minnegev lemaale akrabbim. kol makom shenneemar "venasav" o "veyatza" melammed shello haya hammetzer shave ella holech veyotze lachutz; yotze hammetzer veokem letzad tzefono shel olam, baalachson lammaarav, veover hammetzer bidromah shel maale akrabbim, nimtza maale akrabbim lifnim min hammetzer:
Veavar tzina. el tzin, kemo mitzrayma:
Vehayu totzeotav. ketzotav, bidromah shel kadesh barnea:

Veyatza chatzar addar. mitpashet hammetzer umarchiv letzad tzafon shel olam venimshach od baalachson lammaarav, uva lo lachatzar addar, umisham leatzmon, umisham lenachal mitzrayim; uleshon venasav haamur kan, lefi shekkatav veyatza chatzar addar, shehitchil leharchiv misheavar et kadesh barnea, verochav otah retzua shebbolta letzad tzafon hayeta mikkadesh barnea ad atzmon, umisham vahalea nitkatztzer hammetzer venasav letzad haddarom uva lo lenachal mitzrayim, umisham letzad hammaarav el hayyam haggadol shehu metzer maaravah shel kol eretz yisrael, nimtza shennachal mitzrayim bemiktzoa maaravit deromit:
Vehayu totzeotav hayyamma. el metzer hammaarav sheen od gevul negev maarich letzad hammaarav misham vahalea:
Ugevul yam. umetzer maaravi mahu?
Vehaya lachem hayyam haggadol. lemetzer:
Ugevul. hannissin shebbetoch hayyam af hem min haggevul, vehem iyyim shekkorin ayzls:
Gevul tzafon. metzer tzafon:
Min hayyam haggadol tetau lachem hor hahar. shehu vemiktzoa tzefonit maaravit verosho mashpia venichnas letoch hayyam, veyesh merochav hayyam lifnim hemennu vechutza hemennu:
Tetau. teshappeu lachem, lintot mimmaarav latztzafon, el hor hahar:
Tetau. leshon sibba, kemo "el ta haratzim" (Melachim 1 14), "vetae hashaar" (Yechezkel 40) — hayyatzia, shekkorin apndytz, shehu musav umeshuppa:
Mehor hahar. tasobbu vetelechu el metzer hatztzafon letzad hammizrach, vetifgeu bilvo chamat, zo antocheya:

Totzeot haggevul. sofe haggevul; kol makom shenneemar totzeot haggevul, o hammetzer kale sham legamre veeno over lehallan kelal, o misham mitpashet umarchiv veyotze laachorav lehimmashech lehallan baalachson yoter min harochav harishon, uleinyan rochav hammidda harishon kerao totzaot, shesham kolta otah midda:
Vehayu totzeotav chatzar enan. hu haya sof hammetzer hatztzefoni, venimtzet chatzar enan bemiktzoa tzefonit mizrachit, umisham vahataoitam lakam el metzer hammizrachi:
Vehitavvitem. leshon hasibba unetiyya, kemo "tetau":
Shefama. bammetzer hammizrachi, umisham harivla:
Mikkedem laayin. shem makom, vehammetzer holech bemizracho, nimtza haayin lifnim min hammetzer umeeretz yisrael hu:
Veyarad hagabol. kol shehaggevul holech mitztzafon laddarom hu yored veholech:

Umacha al ketef yam kinneret kedema. sheyyehe yam kinneret toch laggevul, bammaarav, vehaggevul bemizrach yam kinneret, umisham yarad el hayyarden, vehayyarden moshech uva min hatztzafon laddarom baalachson, note letzad mizrach mitkarev letzad eretz kenaan keneged yam kinneret, umoshech letzad mizrachah shel eretz yisrael (keneged yam kinneret) ad shennofel beyam hammelach, umisham kale haggevul betotzeotav el yam hammelach, shemmimmennu hatchalat metzer miktzoa deromit mizrachit, hare sovevet otah learba ruchoteha:

Asher yinchalu lachem. bishvilechem; kol nasi venasi appoteroppos leshivto umechallek nachalat hashevet lammishpachot velaggevarim, uvorer lechol echad veechad chelek hagun, uma shehem osim yihye asuy keillu asaum sheluchim; velo yittachen lefaresh lakam ze kechol lachem shebbammikra, sheim ken haya lo lichtov yanchilu lachem, yinchalu mashma shehem nochalim lachem — bishvilechem uvimkomechem, kemo "Adonai yillachem lachem" (Shemot 14):
Linchol et haaretz. sheyyehe nochel vecholek otah bimkomechem:
Lenachel et bene yisrael. shehem yanchilu otah lachem lemachlekoteha:
Elef amma saviv. veacharav hu omer alpayim amma, ha chetzad? alpayim hu noten lahem saviv, umehem elef happenimiyyim lemigrash vehachitzonim lesadot ucheramim:
Vehikritem. en hakraya ella leshon hazmana, vechen hu omer "ki hikra Adonai elohecha lefanai" (Bereshit 27):
Miggoel. mippene goel haddam, shehu karov lannirtzach:
Shesh are miklat. maggid sheaapi shehivdil moshe bechayyav shalosh arim beever hayyarden, lo hayu koletot ad shennivcharu shalosh shennatan yehoshua beeretz kenaan (Sifre; Makkot 9):

Et shelosh hearim vegomer'. aapi shebbeeretz kenaan tisha shevatim vechan enan ella shenayim vachetzi, hishva minyan are hammiklat shellahem, mishum divgilad nefishe rotzechim, dichtiv (Hoshea 6) "gilad kiryat poale aven akubba middam" (sham):

Veim bichli varzel hikkahu. en ze medabber behoreg beshogeg hassamuch lo, ella behoreg bemezid, uva lelammed shehahoreg bechol davar tzarich sheyyehe vo shiur kede lehamit, shenneemar bechullam "asher yamut bo", dimtargeminan "dehi chemissat dimut beh", chutz min habbarzel, sheggaluy veyadua lifne hakkabbah shehabbarzel memit bechol shehu, afillu machat, lefichach lo notna vo tora shiur lichtov bo asher yamut bo; veim tomar behoreg beshogeg hakkatuv medabber, hare hu omer lematta o bakal even ashar yamot bah bala raot vego', limmed al haamurim lemala shebbehoreg bemezid hakkatuv medabber:
Beeven yad. sheyyesh bah melo yad (sifre):
Asher yamut bah. sheyyesh bah shiur lehamit, ketargumo; lefi shenneemar "vehikka ish et reehu beeven" (Shemot 21), velo natan bah shiur, yachol kol shehu, lechach neemar ashar yamot bah:
O bichli etz yad. lefi shenneemar (sham) "vechi yakke ish et avdo o et amato bashevet", yachol kol shehu, lechach neemar "beetz asher yamut bo" — sheyyehe bo kede lehamit (sifre):
Befigo vo. afillu betoch are miklat:
Bitzdiyya. ketargumo, "bechamna" — bemaarav:
Befeta. beones, vetargumo "bitchef", shehaya samuch lo velo haya lo shahut lehizzaher alav:
O vechol even asher yamut bah. hikkahu:
Belo reot. shello raahu:
Vayyappel alav. mikkan ameru hahoreg derech yerida gole, derech aliyya eno gole (Makkot 30):

Ad mot hakkohen hagadol. shehu va lehashrot shechina veyisrael ulehaarich yemehem, veharotzeach ba lesallek et hashechina miyyisrael umekatztzer et yeme hachayyim, eno cheday sheyyehe lifne kohen gadol (sifre); davar acher — lefi shehaya lo lechohen gadol lehitpallel shello teera takkala zo leyisrael bechayyav (80' Makkot 11):

Asher mashach oto beshemen hakkodesh. lefi feshuto min hammikraot hakketzarim hu, shello peresh mi meshacho, ella kemo asher meshacho hammosheach oto beshemen hakkodesh; verabbotenu derashuhu vemassechet makkot (sham) lirayat davar, lelammed sheim ad shello nigmar dino met hakkohen gadol uminnu acher tachtav, uleachar mikkan nigmar dino, chozer bemitato shel sheni, shenneemar ashar mashach atv, vechi hu moshecho lakkohen o hakkohen mashach oto? ella lehavi et hannimshach beyamav shemmachaziro bemitato:
En lo dam. hare hu kehoreg et hammet, sheen lo dam:
Bechol moshevotechem. limmed shettehe sanhedrin ketanna noheget bechutza laaretz kol zeman shennoheget beeretz yisrael (Makkot 7):
Kol makke nefesh vegomer'. habba leharego al shehikka et hannefesh (80' Sifre):
Lefi edim yirtzach. sheyyaidu shebbemezid uvehatraa harago:
Velo tikchu chofer. lo yippater bemamon (Ketuvot 37):
Velo tikchu chofer lanus el ir miklato. lemi shennas el ir miklat, sheharag beshogeg, eno niftar miggalut bemamon, litten kofer lashob lashabat baratz terem yamut hakkohen (sham):

Lanus. kemo lannas, kemo "shuve milchama" (Micha 2) — sheshavu min hammilchama, vechen "nuge mimmoed" (Tzefanya 3), vechen "ki mulim hayu" (Yehoshua 5); kaasher tomar shuv al mi sheshav kevar, umul al shemmal kevar, ken tomar lanus al mi shennas kevar, vekorehu nus, kelomar muvrach. veim tomar lanus — livroach, utefareshehu lo tikchu chofer lemi sheyyesh lo livroach lefotro min haggalut (80' Sifre), lo yadati heach yomar lashuv lashevet baaretz, hare adayin lo nas, umehechan yashuv?:
Velo tachanifu. lo tarshiu, ketargumo — "vela techayvun":
Asher ani shochen betochah. shello tashkinu oti vetumatah:
Ki ani Adonai shochen betoch bene yisrael. af bizman shehem temeim shechina venehem (sifre):
Venosaf al nachalat hammatte. shehare venah yoreshah, vehabben mityaches al shevet aviv:
Veim yihye hayyovel. mikkan haya ra' yehuda omer atid hayyovel sheyyifsok (Sifra Vayikra 2):

Veim yihye hiobal. kelomar, en zo mechira shechozeret bayyovel, shehayrusha enah chozeret, vaafillu im yihye hayyovel lo tachazor hannachala leshivto, venimtza shennosefa al nachalat hamatah ashar tahiinah laham:
Vechol bat yoreshet nachala. shello haya ven leaviha:
Machla tirtza vegomer'. kan menaan lefi gedullatan zo mizzo bashanim, venisseu keseder toledotan, uvechol hammikra menaan lefi chochmatan, umaggid sheshekulot zo kezo (80' Bava Batra 120):

Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:63-: And the wise person, whose eyes are in his head, shall weigh whether occupying himself with Torah at the time of prayer is greater or answering "amen," and without doubt they are not of the same category at the time of prayer, for "a word in its proper time, how good it is." And it appears to me that Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi intended this and said, happy is he whose toil is in Torah and gives satisfaction to his Maker (Berachot 17a) - that his toil in Torah be a satisfaction to his Maker - to exclude one who occupies himself with Torah at a time when the Holy One, blessed be He, has no desire for his Torah, in the aspects mentioned - then certainly there is no satisfaction to the Holy One, blessed be He, in his Torah, and it would be better for him not to occupy himself with Torah [then].

And just as one must be careful throughout the prayer leader's repetition not to speak, so one must be careful on Sabbath eve when the prayer leader repeats "Vayechulu," as it is written in Sefer Chasidim: a certain pious man saw another pious man like himself who had died, with his face yellow. He said to him, why is your face yellow? He said to him, because I would speak during "Vayechulu" at the time the congregation says it, and during the blessing "Magen Avot" while it was being said, and during "Yitgadal" - to this point. So Rabbi Yaakov copied this wording (Tur, Orach Chaim, siman 268).

Further, one must be careful not to speak during the reading of the Torah scroll, and they were strict about this in the Zohar - see there (Parashat Pinchas, page 229a), in these words, in Parashat Vayakhel (page 206a): when the Torah scroll is raised there, then all the people must arrange themselves in fear, in awe, in trembling and quaking, all below, and direct their hearts as though they now stand at Mount Sinai to receive the Torah, and be attentive and incline their ears - and no one, neither the people nor anyone else, has permission to open his mouth in Torah, all the more so in another matter, but rather all in fear, as though he had no mouth - and this has been established, as it is written (Nehemiah 8:5), "and when he opened it, all the people stood," and so on, "and the ears of all the people were toward the book of the Torah" (ibid. 8:3) - to this point.

Further, one must be careful, when occupied with Torah or prayer, to utter the words of Torah and prayer properly, and not say them in haste and swallowed - and they said in the Zohar (Parashat Pinchas, page 227a) that just as the body benefits from bread after the wheat is ground and the fine flour separated from the bran and all the husks, so one must grind the words of Torah with one's teeth until the soul benefits from them - in these words: the thin third husk corresponds to the bran of the wheat, for it clings to the wheat and cannot be separated from it until they grind it in millstones, which correspond to the grinding of the mouth - for a person must grind the words of Torah with them until they become like fine, clean flour, and with a sieve, which is the lip, the refuse, which is the bran of Torah, is separated, until a clean, fine-flour halachah is found - at that time the heart and the brain and all the limbs of the body, in which the soul spreads, take it - in the manner that the body is nourished with worldly things, for "one corresponding to the other, God has made" - the bread of the body and the bread of Torah - this is what is written (Proverbs 9:5), "come, eat of my bread" - to this point.

Further there (Zohar, Parashat Pinchas, page 236a): from here, whoever utters words of Torah must grind them with his teeth and bring forth complete words, and these words are called "complete" - but others, who are fools, who eat words by gulping and do not grind them with their own grinding and with their teeth - what is written of them? (Numbers 11:33), "the meat was yet between their teeth," and so on, "and the anger of the LORD burned against the people" - for they were of the stock of the one who said, "let me gulp down [some of that red stuff]" (Genesis 25:30) - to this point. And this is also brought in this wording in the same passage (Zohar, Parashat Pinchas, page 246a) - see there.

Further, one must be careful, while occupied with Torah, not to interrupt it with conversation, for this is like mixing the profane with something holy, and its punishment is severe - as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Shelach Lecha, page 162a), that a heavenly voice says three things in the Garden of Eden every day, before Bezalel begins to reveal the secrets of the wise, and one of them is, whoever interrupts shall be interrupted - explained as: whoever interrupts words of Torah for idle words, his life shall be interrupted from this world, and his judgment stands in that world - to this point.

And this is what they said in the chapter "Ein Dorshin" (Chagigah 8b): Rabbi Levi said, whoever interrupts words of Torah and occupies himself with idle conversation is fed the coals of broom, as it is said (Job 30:4), "who pluck saltwort by the bushes, and the roots of broom are their food" - and Rashi, peace be upon him, explained in Tractate Avodah Zarah, first chapter (3b), that "who interrupts for idle conversation" - "saltwort" [maluach] is words of moisture, and essentially, another interpretation, "written on tablets." And "coals of broom" was explained in the previous chapter, in the name of Rashi, peace be upon him, concerning the matter of (Psalms 120:4), "sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of broom" - see there.

And the reason for this is that the Torah is fire, and was given in fire, as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:2), "from His right hand went a fiery law for them" - and speaking idle words is fiery coals, for speech comes from the fire of the heart, and when a person is occupied with Torah, his voice hews flames of fire in holiness - however, when he is occupied with idle conversation, it is a foreign fire, and therefore, "in his net which he hid, his own foot is caught" - by the fire of blemish, fire shall consume him.

And in the reason for "whoever interrupts, and so on," is because the Torah is your life and the length of your days - your life in this world, and length of days in the World to Come (cf. Tanchuma, Shemini 11) - and therefore, measure for measure, he has a punishment in this world and in the World to Come.

And when a person, in his occupation with Torah, places the fear of the Holy One, blessed be He, before him, he shall not come to interrupt - as they said, of blessed memory, in Midrash Eichah, on the verse (Lamentations 2:19), "pour out your heart like water before the presence of the LORD," in these words: any Torah scholar who sits alone by himself and reads and studies, it is as though the Holy One, blessed be He, sits opposite him and reads and studies with him - therefore it says "before the presence [nochach penei] of the LORD," and further on it says (1 Kings 20:29), "and these encamped opposite [nochach] these" - to this point.

And with this the chapter is concluded, and we have included the particular aspects of speech one must be careful of, according to the shortness of our understanding - and whoever adds further to such fences, may the blessing of good come upon him:

After we said, in the previous chapters, that the matter of speech depends on the mouth, we wish to speak and, connected to this matter, [address] the holiness of eating, which depends on the mouth - for King Solomon, peace be upon him, mentioned the guarding of the mouth in saying (Proverbs 21:23), "he who guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles," and it is explained in Parashat Shemini (Zohar, page 41a-b), whose wording we copied in chapter 11, that "his mouth" means the guarding of his mouth from impure foods. And with God's help we shall explain the aspects of the holiness of eating in what is permitted, according to what is found in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, and the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, and the words of the commentators.

Just as our holy Torah mentions the word "holiness" concerning forbidden relations (Leviticus 20:7), and likewise concerning tzitzit (Numbers 15:40) and other places, as we explained at the beginning of this Gate, so it mentions it concerning foods - and therefore, at the end of Parashat Shemini, having mentioned the permitted and forbidden foods, it says there (Leviticus 11:44), "and you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy... and you shall not make yourselves detestable." And the Zohar explains this matter, that upon the impure foods the Torah warns us of, an external and impure spirit rests, and therefore whoever eats of these things defiles his soul and shows about himself that he has no part in holiness or in the God of Israel, for the impure thing becomes part of a limb within the person's very body, and the soul clothes itself there - it follows that he defiles his soul and defiles the soul clothed in the body. And through this the wording of the Zohar is precise, saying, whoever eats of those forbidden foods becomes attached to the Other Side and defiles his soul and his body, and an impure spirit rests upon him - and its saying "his soul and his body" teaches what has been said. And they elaborate further there on the punishment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:15-: And further, they said, of blessed memory, in Berachot (29b): Elijah said to Rav Yehudah, brother of Rav Sala, do not become angry and you will not sin; do not become drunk and you will not sin. Rabbeinu Yonah's disciples explain "do not become drunk and you will not sin" as meaning, and do not become full [sated], so that you not come to sin - for when a person is full and drawn after his pleasures, he forgets the matters of the blessed Creator. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explains "do not become drunk" as, do not become intoxicated with wine - and the law is with him, for the Targum on (Genesis 9:21), "and he drank of the wine and became drunk," is "veshati min chamra u-revi," and likewise "shikor yayin" [drunk with wine] is "meravi chamra" - except that Rabbeinu Yonah's disciples' explanation may also be reconciled, since generally a person only becomes intoxicated from an abundance of eating, when he is full - and thus both explanations are correct.

And further it says in Bereshit Rabbah (38:7), concerning the generation of the dispersion, in these words: Rav Chelbo said, wherever you find satisfaction of spirit, Satan accuses; Rabbi Levi said, wherever you find eating and drinking, Satan accuses - to this point.

And in the Midrash HaNe'elam (Zohar, Parashat Chayei Sarah, page 127a), it says, concerning the resurrection of the dead, concerning (Genesis 24:4), "but you shall take a wife for my son from there" - Rabbi Yitzchak said, that body which suffered with me in that world and had no pleasure and yearned for it out of fear of its Maker, that body I shall take for Isaac - to this point, relevant here. And from this it appears explicitly that whoever suffers and distances himself from pleasures fears the LORD, as it says, "out of fear of its Maker" - and the intent is that he does not wish to enjoy so as not to come to sin, for pleasure brings one to sin, as we have explained and shall further explain, with God's help. See, see indeed how much one must distance himself from the husk of pleasures and subdue it.

And at the end of the teaching it says, happy is he who derives no benefit at all from its own - it changed its wording, for above it said "did not delight" from its own, and here it says "derives no benefit" from its own. And the intent is to inform us that there is an additional virtue for one who has not even a slight benefit from the husk, all the more so pleasure - and this is the nature of the phrase "happy is he" [zakai hu] - meaning an additional, greater virtue. And this is the way my teacher, peace be upon him, followed - wherever the Zohar says "zakai hu," it indicates something more excellent than what preceded.

And its explanation that he has no benefit is that he content himself with a small amount for the sustenance of the soul - and this is "the sustenance of a Torah scholar," which Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Parashat Beshalach, page 62a), whose wording we copied above, "happy is the portion of the body that can be nourished with the food of the soul." And it appears to me that the intent is that that husk, which is the husk of the worm, shall not rule over him - therefore a person must distance himself from this hard husk, which is what causes a person to pursue eating and drinking.

And Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, author of Menorat HaMaor, wrote (part 2, letter 17), in these words: because of the lowliness of his name, the wicked person who pursues eating and drinking is called "Oy Val" [woe and futility], an acronym of "eat, drink, he shall say to you" (Proverbs 23:7) - for he thinks this world was created only for eating and drinking, and those who pursue their desire, today satiate themselves with what is permitted, and tomorrow with what is forbidden - and when they cannot obtain it from their own, they steal from others - and concerning this the Torah commanded the matter of the wayward and rebellious son, that he be killed if his father saw him eat two tartemars of meat and half a log of Italian wine - for since he has begun pursuing pleasures, he shall come to consume his father's property, and if he does not find it, he shall come to rob people - and it is better that he die innocent rather than die guilty - so they said in the chapter "Sorer U-Moreh" (Sanhedrin 72a).

Therefore one must be careful not to pursue excesses, for excessive eating is what brings a person to sin, and immediately his inclination becomes proud over him - as they said in the Sifrei (Ha'azinu, piska 13), in these words, on (Deuteronomy 32:15), "and Jeshurun grew fat and kicked" - from satiety they rebel. And so you find concerning the generation of the Flood, that they did not rebel before the Omnipresent except through food, drink, and tranquility - what is said of them? (Genesis 11:1), "and the whole earth was of one language." And so we find concerning the men of the [Tower of Babel], that they did not rebel before the Omnipresent, and so on - and so it says (Ezekiel 16:48), "as I live, says the LORD, Sodom your sister has not done, she and her daughters, as you have done." You find concerning the men of the wilderness generation, that they did not rebel before the Omnipresent except through food, as it is said (Exodus 32:6), "and the people sat down to eat and drink" - what is said of them? (ibid. 32:8), "they have turned aside quickly from the way." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, tell Israel, when you enter the land, you shall rebel against Me only through eating and drinking, as it is said (Deuteronomy 31:20), "for when I shall bring them into the land which I swore to their fathers, flowing with milk and honey, and they shall eat and be satisfied and grow fat, then they shall turn to other gods." Moses said to Israel, when you enter the land, you shall rebel only through eating and drinking, as it is said (ibid. 8:12), "lest you eat and be satisfied, and build good houses," and so on, "and your herds and flocks multiply" - what is said of them? (ibid. 8:14), "then your heart shall be lifted up, and you shall forget the LORD your God." And so you find concerning Job's sons and daughters, that calamity came upon them only through eating, drinking, and tranquility, as it is said (Job 1:18), "while he was yet speaking, another also came and said, your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking wine... and behold, a great wind." And so you find concerning the ten tribes, that they were exiled only through eating, drinking, and tranquility, as it is said (Amos 6:6), "who lie upon beds of ivory... who drink wine in bowls... therefore now they shall be exiled at the head of those who go into exile" - and they elaborate further there - to this point, relevant here.

And in the Tosefta of Sotah, chapter 3 (siman 3), they prove all this from the verses concerning the men of the Tower, as it is said (Genesis 11:2), "and it came to pass, as they journeyed from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they dwelt [vayeshvu] there" - and "dwelling" [yeshivah] refers only to eating and drinking, as it is said, "and the people sat down [vayeshev] to eat and drink" (Exodus 32:6) - it was this that caused them, "and they said," and so on. The men of Sodom did not become haughty before the Omnipresent except through the good He bestowed upon them, as it is said (Job 28:7), "a path that no bird of prey knows... a land from which bread comes forth... a place whose stones are sapphires." The men of Sodom said, since food comes forth from our land, and silver and gold come forth from our land, and precious stones and pearls come forth from our land, we do not need people to come to us, for they only diminish us - let us stand and abolish the practice [of hospitality] from among us. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, when I did good to you, you sought to abolish the practice [of hospitality] from among you - I shall abolish the practice from among you and forget you from the world. What does it say? (ibid. 12:6), "the tents of robbers prosper... those who provoke God are secure" - and so it says (Ezekiel 16:48), "as I live, says the LORD, Sodom your sister has not done... behold, this was the iniquity of Sodom your sister: pride, fullness of bread," and so on - to this point.

And just as one must be careful of excessive eating, so one must be careful of excessive wine - for a little of it benefits the stomach and gives clarity, as they said, of blessed memory (Horayot 13b), "wine and fragrances make [scholars] clear-minded" - but one who becomes drunk with it destroys his body and loses his mind, and it causes him all the evils in the world, as we find concerning Noah, that it caused him harm and disgrace, and became a cause for him to curse his own descendants, as we read in Sanhedrin (70a): the Galilean expounded, thirteen "vav"s [connective "and"s, punning on "vai," woe] are stated concerning wine (Genesis 9:20-24): "and Noah, a man of the earth, began [vayachel]," "and he planted a vineyard," "and he drank of the wine," "and he became drunk," "and he uncovered himself," "and Ham saw," "and he told his two brothers," "and Shem and Japheth took," "and they placed it on the shoulders of both of them," "and they went," "and they covered," "and Noah awoke from his wine," "and he knew what his youngest son had done to him" - to this point. And it appears to me that the intent of these thirteen "vav"s is that they are all "vav-yud" [connective forms], to indicate "oy, vai" [woe, alas], and they are thirteen, to indicate a blemish in unity, for "echad" [one] totals thirteen. And further, thirteen times "vav" totals seventy-eight, corresponding to the numerical value of the three Names "YHVH Melech YHVH," and so on. And there is proof for this from what is said there, further: the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Noah, should you not have learned from the first man, whom only wine caused [to sin]? As they said in the Midrash, that tree from which the first man ate was a grapevine, for there is nothing that brings wailing into the world upon a person like wine - to this point. Behold, it says that the sin of the first man was in it, and they said, of blessed memory, that a taint of disqualification was cast into the first man in that sin - and it says "there is nothing that brings wailing," precise about the language of "vai" [woe].

And further we say there in Tractate Eruvin (65a): Rabbi Chanan said, wine was created in this world only to comfort mourners and to pay reward to the wicked, as it is said (Proverbs 31:6), "give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those of bitter soul." Rabbi said, what is written (ibid. 23:31), "do not look upon wine when it is red, when it gives its color in the cup"? Do not look at wine, which makes the faces of the wicked red in this world, but in the end whitens their faces in the World to Come. Rava said, "do not look upon wine when it is red" - for its end is blood. Rav Kahana raised a difficulty: it is written "yesamech" [without the letter he, defective spelling] but read as "yesamach" - if he merits, it gladdens him; if he does not merit, it makes him desolate - and this is what Rava said, "wine and fragrances make [scholars] clear-minded" - to this point.

Further, they said in Midrash Mishlei, on the verse (Proverbs 23:29), "who has woe, who has sorrow" - Rabbi Simon said, come and see how severe wine is, that thirteen "vav"s are stated concerning wine at the beginning, and so on, as expounded. And it says afterward, Solomon came and explained in his wisdom, "who has woe, who has sorrow" - this is one who becomes drunk, woe to him and to his father, as it is said (Deuteronomy 21:18), "if a man has a wayward and rebellious son." "Who has strife" - because he becomes drunk with his wine, he reveals a secret between one person and another, and he sows discord. "Who has complaint" - because he becomes drunk with his wine, he speaks excessively, and so on. "Who has wounds without cause" - because he becomes drunk with his wine, he goes and makes a wound and a bruise. "Without cause," why? Because there is no judgment against him [he is too drunk to be held responsible]. "Who has redness of eyes" - one who drank as much as he needed - this is what is written (Genesis 49:12), "his eyes red from wine, and his teeth white from milk" - Rabbi Yirmiyah said, do not read "u-lvan shinayim" [white of teeth] but "lavan sanim" [whitens those who hate him] - just as milk pacifies an infant's mind, so wine restores an elder's mind.

What is written after it? (Proverbs 23:30), "those who tarry long over wine, those who go to seek out mixed wine" - Rabbi Elazar said, woe to him who neglects words of Torah and rises early for wine. What is written after it? "Do not look upon wine when it is red, when it gives its color in the cup [ba-kos]" - Rabbi Yochanan said, it is written "ba-kis" [in the purse] but read "ba-kos" [in the cup] - and why is this? The buyer sets his eyes on the cup, and the seller sets his eye on the purse. And in Vayikra Rabbah (12:1) it explains the completion of the verse explicitly: "it goes down smoothly" - in the end he turns his house into a level plain [ruined] - from this copper pot he makes a clay pot, a servant sells it and drinks wine with its price - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:27-: What is written after it? (ibid. 23:32), "in the end it bites like a serpent, and stings like a viper" - just as the serpent bites and kills and separates between death and life, so wine separates between death and life - to this point.

Further, they said, "lest he drink and forget mechukak [that which is decreed]" (Proverbs 31:5) - "mechukak" totals two hundred forty-eight, meaning that through drinking wine he shall forget to fulfill the two hundred forty-eight positive commandments - in these words: "lest he drink and forget mechukak" - whoever drinks much wine eventually forgets in his two hundred forty-eight limbs - this is what is written, "lest he drink and forget mechukak" - written "mechukak," and they [total] two hundred forty-eight. Rabbi Chanina bar Papa said, the Holy One, blessed be He, said, I had a great House and destroyed it only because of wine. And the Rabbis say, I had two princes [Nadav and Avihu] and they died only because of wine, for Rabbi Yishmael taught, the two sons of Aaron died only because they entered [the sanctuary] having drunk wine - to this point. "He shall drink and forget mechukak" - Rabbi Shimon said, these are the words of Torah, which are engraved [chakukim], and it is written concerning them (Exodus 20:13), "you shall not commit adultery." Further it says, he shall forget the Torah given through the lawgiver [mechokek] - this is Moses, as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:21), "for there the portion of the lawgiver [mechokek] was hidden away" - to this point.

Further, in Midrash Rabbah, Parashat Nazir (Bamidbar Rabbah 10:2), in these words: "do not look upon wine when it is red" (23:31) - the holy spirit warned concerning wine, that a person not become drunk - why? "When it gives its color" - for its end is blood, that he commit a transgression for which he is liable to death. Another interpretation, "for he shall lust after" the blood of a menstruant and the blood of a woman with a flux. "When it gives its color in the cup" - written "in the purse" - through the cup he shall give his eye to the purse - the Torah spoke in refined language, meaning that he shall come upon forbidden relations. "It goes down smoothly" - in the end his wife says, I saw it like a red rose [i.e., signs suggesting adultery] and he does not separate from her [investigate]. Rabbi Asi said, if he is a Torah scholar, in the end he declares the pure impure and the impure pure. Another interpretation, "it goes down smoothly" - in the end he permits transgressions and treats them as ownerless, like a level plain - he converses with a woman in the marketplace, speaks vulgarly in his drunkenness, and is not ashamed.

"In the end it bites like a serpent" - just as the serpent, by enticing Eve to drink wine [i.e., eat the fruit], caused the ground to be cursed because of it, as it is said (Genesis 3:17), "cursed is the ground because of you" - so, through wine, a third of the world was cursed, as it is said (ibid. 9:24), "and Noah awoke from his wine," and so on, (ibid. 9:25), "cursed be Canaan" - this was Ham, who was his third son, and he is called the father of Canaan, and therefore they were cursed. Just as the viper separates between death and life, so wine separates a person from the ways of life to the ways of death, since wine causes him to come to idolatry - this is what is written (Proverbs 23:33), "your eyes shall see strange things [zarot]" - as it is written (Psalms 81:10), "there shall be no strange god [el zar] in you." Another interpretation, that he comes upon a married woman, as it is said (Proverbs 5:20), "and why should you, my son, go astray with a strange woman [zarah]?" - to this point. And from the sum of the teaching you learn that wine causes idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed.

Further there, another interpretation, that it makes the commandments strange, as it is said (Proverbs 21:24), "proud, haughty, scoffer is his name, who acts with insolent pride [za'don]" - this is a drunkard, who is called haughty and a scoffer. "Haughty" - from where? As it is said (Habakkuk 2:5), "moreover, wine is a traitor, a haughty man, and he does not stay home." "Scoffer" - from where? As it is written (Proverbs 20:1), "wine is a scoffer, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise" - behold, he is also called a scoffer - and you already know that the group of scoffers does not receive the countenance of the Shechinah (Sanhedrin 103a). Further there, "and your heart shall speak perverse things" (Proverbs 23:33) - for he turns his face away from the Holy One, blessed be He, and from the commandments, as it is said (Deuteronomy 32:20), "for they are a perverse generation," and so on.

"And you shall be like one who lies down in the midst of the sea" (Proverbs 23:34) - this is Noah, who lay in the ark for twelve months amid the waters of the Flood, and because he drank and became drunk, an unfitness happened to him, that he was castrated [by Ham]. "And like one who lies at the top of a mast" - this is the primordial man [Adam], who is the head of all people, upon whom death was decreed because of wine, and who caused death's pangs to be brought into the world.

"They struck me, and I felt no hurt" (Proverbs 23:35) - woe to the adulterer who does not learn wisdom from what happened to him - he saw what happened to the "sotah" [suspected adulteress] through wine, and did not learn wisdom. "They beat me, and I did not know it" - he saw in the Torah what happened to the adulterer through wine, and did not know how to understand, but rather said, "when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again" - for as long as he has leisure to occupy himself with licentiousness, he pursues it. Behold, we have learned that wine causes licentiousness, and therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, wrote in the Torah the portion of the Nazirite after the portion of the "sotah" - so that a person not do the deed of the adulterer and adulteress, who drank wine and were corrupted, but rather one who fears sin shall make himself a Nazirite from wine - therefore it is said (Numbers 6:2), "if a man or woman shall set apart" - to this point.

And what we find in the Talmud, "wine and fragrances make [scholars] clear-minded" - this refers to wine in small amount, well diluted; but undiluted wine is what is harmful - and so it is understood there in Midrash Bamidbar Rabbah - see there - and we shall not copy its wording so as not to be lengthy.

And the end of his words there teaches you that no good comes out of wine. And especially students of Torah must be careful of excessive wine, and that wine brings on sleep - and our Sages, of blessed memory, said in Sanhedrin (chapter 8, mishnah 5), "wine and sleep for the wicked - good for them and good for the world; for the righteous - bad for them and bad for the world" - for wine is harmful for the righteous, because it increases sleep and they come to be idle from the words of Torah. And this is why King Solomon, peace be upon him, after condemning wine, praised wisdom, saying (Proverbs 24:1), "do not envy evil men, nor desire to be with them," and so on, and afterward said (24:3), "through wisdom a house is built," and said (24:5), "a wise man is strong, and a man of knowledge increases strength," and afterward said (24:10), "if you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small" - and they said, of blessed memory, in Midrash Mishlei on this verse, Rabbi Abahu said, whoever weakens himself from the words of Torah has no strength to stand in the day of adversity - and in the Zohar, Parashat Vayetze (page 152b), they elaborate in explaining this verse, and we shall copy it in its place. It follows that wine is, for a Torah scholar, a cause for him to grow weak in the words of Torah.

And you shall find that they said in the Mishnah (Ta'anit, chapter 2, mishnah 7), the men of the priestly watch are permitted to drink wine at night but not by day, while the men of the ancestral house [officiating that day] are forbidden neither by day nor by night. And Rashi explains: "at night," there is no concern that the service might become too heavy, for they saw already in the evening that the offerings had ceased and the service was not heavy. "Not by day," for many offerings might come and the men of the ancestral house would not suffice for that whole day, and these [the watch] would need to assist them, and they would be unfit for service because of drunkenness. "The men of the ancestral house, neither by day nor by night," because they would spend the whole night bringing up limbs and fats that had fallen off the altar, or, if they had not finished by day, they would finish at night - but the men of the watch do not need to assist at night in turning with the fork, for the ancestral house can suffice alone for turning the arrangement [of wood] - to this point. We find, then, that we learn that whoever's service was heavy upon them was forbidden wine, so that they not come to be idle from the service. And so whoever wishes to bear the yoke of Torah and not come to be idle from it should distance himself from wine.

And they said in the Midrash HaNe'elam (Zohar, Parashat Vayera, beginning of page 110), in these words: Rabbi Yitzchak said, the evil inclination is never enticed except through eating and drinking, and through the joy of wine it then rules over a person. Concerning the righteous, what is written of him? (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul," and he never becomes drunk - for Rabbi Yehudah said, this young Torah scholar who becomes drunk, I apply to him (ibid. 11:22), "a gold ring in a pig's snout," and not only that, but he desecrates the Name of Heaven. What is the practice of the wicked? "Behold joy and gladness" (Isaiah 22:13) - wine then rules over a person - "slaying oxen and killing sheep," and so on (Isaiah, ibid.) - and concerning them Scripture says (Isaiah 5:11), "woe to those who rise early in the morning to pursue strong drink" - in order to arouse the evil inclination, for the evil inclination is aroused only through wine, as it is said (Genesis 19:33), "and they made their father drink wine" - to this point.

And concerning the intent of eating and drinking, by the plain meaning, Rabbi Yisrael, peace be upon him, wrote in Sefer Menorat HaMaor that one should be happy with his portion, and trust in his Maker that He will provide his sustenance, and not restrict himself with the exactitudes of poverty. And so they said in the Midrash, "all the days of the poor are evil" - meaning, whoever is poor in his faith and grows weary of expense, and if he acquires livelihood for himself, fears that he will decline in his possessions and need people - he is found in sorrow and worry all his days; but whoever is happy with his portion and believes in the Holy One, blessed be He, that He shall provide his sustenance whenever he needs it, his heart is always joyful and of good cheer, as though a table were set and a feast were always before him. And further we read in the Midrash, "better a dry morsel with quiet than [a house full of feasting with strife]" (Proverbs 17:1) - this is one who is happy with his portion, and shall always be at ease and tranquil, since he is happy with what the Holy One, blessed be He, provided him; he shall never steal or rob, and is found calm and confident all his days. "Than a house full of sacrifices with strife" - this is one who is not happy with his portion, but pursues coarse foods, and steals and robs to satisfy his desire, and is found all his days in strife and quarrel and pursued by people. And one who eats little to satisfy his soul and does not intend his own bodily benefit recognizes his Creator - for when he hungers he shall understand his own lack and the lowliness of man, that at the time he lacks a portion of bread and a jug of water, his strength and all his limbs weaken, his eyes darken, and he lacks the strength to stand on his feet - and then he shall recognize the perfection of the Holy One, blessed be He, who needs neither eating nor drinking, as it is said (Psalms 50:13), "shall I eat the flesh of bulls," and so on. And when he hungers he shall lift his eyes to the Holy One, blessed be He, to seek his sustenance, and know that He, blessed be His Name, gives bread to all flesh, and provides sustenance for each and every one, and for every single body enough for its lack. And then he shall have mercy on the poor and separate from pride, since coarse foods bring a person to sins and guilt, as it is said (Deuteronomy 32:15), "and Jeshurun grew fat and kicked," and it is written (ibid. 11:15), "and you shall eat and be satisfied - take heed to yourselves," and so on.

And what is praiseworthy in a person concerning eating is three things: the first, that he content himself with his portion, even a little, and not seek more; second, that he eat at its proper time, before he becomes very hungry and his limbs weaken and he comes to illness, and has no strength to serve the Holy One, blessed be He, properly, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 10:16), "and your princes eat in the morning"; third, that he not intend in his eating his bodily pleasure but only the sustenance of his soul, and not follow his desire to eat everything his palate craves, evil foods, because they are harmful. And Ramban, of blessed memory, wrote that a person should always eat less than a third [of what would satisfy him]. And they said, of blessed memory (Gittin 70a), a meal from which you derive pleasure, withdraw your hand from it - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:3-1: So too, one who eats his food for the sake of Heaven, as shall be explained, and from the things the Torah permitted, upon which rests a spirit of righteousness, holiness, and purity - the soul enjoys that eating from the aspect of holiness within it - and this is (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul." For by the plain sense of the verse it is difficult - what is "to satisfy his soul"? For the soul is spiritual and holy, and is not satisfied by this physical eating but only by the eating of Torah - and so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Beshalach, page 62b), that "his soul's satisfaction" is the spiritual eating, which is the eating of Torah, in these words: it says there that a person should not eat until he has prayed for his sustenance, and they said, of blessed memory, Rabbi Yitzchak said, from here (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - after his soul is satisfied from praying and reading Torah - to this point. Behold, it says "his soul's satisfaction" according to the truth, namely the spiritual satisfaction pertaining to the soul - however, in what we explained, that in the eating itself there is an aspect of holiness, from that aspect of holiness the soul is satisfied.

And therefore it is fitting for a person to be strict with himself concerning his own food, that it have no aspect of prohibition at all - for the prophet Ezekiel would praise himself for not eating from an animal that a sage ruled on, even though it was permitted, since a doubt of prohibition arose concerning it - as they said, of blessed memory, in the chapter "Elu Treifot" (Chullin 37b), on the verse (Ezekiel 4:14), "nor did piggul flesh come into my mouth" - all the more so if there is an aspect of prohibition in the food itself, it is fitting to distance oneself from it. And there are several matters where a dispute arose among the later authorities as to whose ruling is halachah, one forbidding and one permitting - and certainly the prophet Ezekiel, peace be upon him, would not eat such a thing, for the one who forbids it treats it as a piece of forbidden matter, and it is more severe than one on which a sage has [merely] ruled [that it is permitted]. And it is written in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Repentance, chapter 5) that the pious would abstain from seventy gates of the gates of the permitted, out of their fear of one gate of the gates of the forbidden.

And similarly one must be careful in several other matters, not to buy things that carry a suspicion of prohibition except from an honest Jew who is meticulous about it properly - for if he is suspected of it, he is not trusted, as we learn at the end of chapter 4 of Bechorot (mishnah 10): this is the general rule, whoever is suspected of a matter is neither judged by it nor testifies concerning it - and this matter applies particularly to bread, wine, meat, milk, cheese, and grape honey, and anything involving the cooking of gentiles, except what the halachic authorities have explicitly permitted.

And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained in Midrash Mishlei, on the verse (Proverbs 21:23 - actually 13:25), "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul," several explanations, all coming to one path, in these words: another interpretation, "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - this is Eliezer, servant of Abraham, who said to our mother Rebecca (Genesis 24:17), "please let me sip a little water from your jug" - one sip. "But the belly of the wicked shall want" - this is Esau the wicked, who said to our father Jacob (ibid. 25:30), "let me gulp down, please, some of that red stuff" - that wicked one opened his mouth wide like a camel and said, open my mouth and let it flow in, empty the whole pot into it, as we have learned (Shabbat, chapter 24, mishnah 3), one may not stuff a camel [with a lot at once] nor force-feed it by pressing, but one may pour food into its mouth [to gulp].

Another interpretation, "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - this is Ruth the Moabite, as it is written (Ruth 2:14), "and she ate, and was satisfied, and left over." Rabbi Yitzchak said, from this you hear two things - either a blessing rested in that righteous man's [Boaz's] hand, or a blessing rested in the belly of that righteous woman - from the fact that it is written "and she ate, and was satisfied, and left over," it appears that the blessing rested in the belly of the righteous woman. "But the belly of the wicked shall want" - these are the nations of the world, idol worshippers, and so on.

Another interpretation, "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - this is Hezekiah king of Judah - they said of Hezekiah king of Judah that he would eat two bundles of vegetables, and one litra of meat was brought before him every day, and Israel slandered him and said, this is a king, and Retzin is a king - the delight and kingship fitting for Retzin son of Remaliah - this is what is written (Isaiah 8:6), "because this people has despised the waters of Shiloah that flow gently" - this is Hezekiah king of Judah, who would purify Israel in a mikveh of forty se'ah, corresponding to the numerical value of "le'at" [gently] - the Holy One, blessed be He, said, you bring up food and are satisfied [with little], therefore behold, the LORD brings up upon you the waters of the river. "But the belly of the wicked shall want" - this is Mesha king of Moab, who was a sheep-breeder - and what is "noked"? A shepherd, as it is said (2 Kings 3:4), "and Mesha king of Moab was a sheep-breeder," and so on. And in the Yalkut (Mishlei, siman 950, page 138, col. 2) it is brought in another manner, "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - this is Hezekiah, as stated; "but the belly of the wicked shall want" - this is Pekach son of Remaliah, who would eat three hundred fledgling birds as dessert after a meal - to this point.

Another interpretation, "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - these are the kings of Israel and the house of David; "but the belly of the wicked shall want" - these are the kings of the East, for whom a hundred sheep would be brought up for each and every one. Another interpretation, "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - this is the Holy One, blessed be He, who said to Israel, My children, of all the offerings you offer before Me, do I derive any benefit from them except the pleasing aroma? - to this point.

Behold, it appears from this teaching the virtue of the righteous, who content themselves with little, and the wicked, who are not satisfied with little - and the reason is that their belly is lacking, that the whole world would not suffice to fill their belly, and it appears in their eyes that their belly is never full.

And when a person sees that everything he adds to his eating adds flesh for the worm, which is his end, certainly it is fitting to distance himself from excessive eating except particularly on Sabbaths and festivals - for whoever indulges in eating and drinking on the six weekdays more than needed for the sustenance of his soul and body is punished, and concerning them it is said (Malachi 2:3), "and I will spread dung on your faces, the dung of your festivals." And it is explained in Tractate Shabbat (151b), on this verse - Rav Huna said, these are those who neglect the words of Torah and make all their days like festivals - and it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel, page 199b), whose wording we copied in the Gate of Fear, chapter 12, that after three days his belly bursts, and they throw the dung on his face, and say to him, take what you chose, and made all your days like festivals and appointed times - see there.

And further, they said in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, page 141a), in these words: the bodies of the righteous, who were not drawn in this world after the pleasures of that strong husk, an impure spirit does not rule over them at all, for they did not participate at all in this world after that strong husk and its pleasures and delights, and they are prepared - such a one is not defiled after his soul departs from him. The bodies of the righteous, who delight in this world only in the pleasures of a commandment and the meals of Sabbaths, festivals, and appointed times - that impure spirit cannot rule over them, for they did not delight in its own [pleasures] at all - since they took nothing of its own, it has no permission over them at all - happy is he who derives no benefit at all from its own - to this point.

Behold, it is explained that whoever delights in meals that are not from Sabbaths and festivals delights from the husk, and the husk rules over him at his death - and this husk is the hard husk of the nut, which is the second husk, and therefore it is called the "strong husk," as explained above that the first husk of the nut is soft.

And the reason pleasures are in this hard husk is because everything a person eats beyond the sustenance of the soul is pleasure, and he adds flesh to his body for the worm - and the reason is that according to how much he is drawn after the worm, which is the husk, the husk shall rule over him, for the flesh of the body in man is drawn from the skin of the serpent, as explained in the Tikkunim (page 42), in these words: at the time Pharaoh's daughter touched him [Moses], the Shechinah flew from him, and therefore, when he wished to draw near her at the burning bush, she said to him, do not come closer, until he strip off that body which Pharaoh's daughter had touched - there it was shown to him that a person's body in this world is leprosy from the skin of the serpent; afterward, when he stripped it off and returned to the Garden of Eden, he was clothed in his own holy body, and this is "and behold, it had returned like his flesh" (cf. Exodus 4:7) - to this point, relevant here. And there is no entry for the external force to cause sin except from the aspect of food, for Samael and his groups are spiritual and man is physical, and they have no entry or relation to attach to him - but when a person is drawn after his desire, he gives a portion to his flesh, which is made from a putrid drop, which is from the husk, and through this he causes it to sin - as it says in the Tikkunim (page 53b), that all sins are from the limbs of the putrid drop, and they say there that the putrid drop is an evil maidservant - and therefore it is said in the Sifrei (Ha'azinu, piska 13), as we shall copy its wording below, that a person rebels only through eating and drinking.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:40-: And the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot, of blessed memory (Gate of Abstinence, chapter 5), wrote concerning abstinence in eating, in these words: and it is fitting for you, my brother, to conduct yourself with abstinence from the permitted pleasures within your ability, until they appear in your eyes like the nature of pleasures forbidden to you - meaning, like [forbidden] fat and the like - lest you abandon your Torah and neglect your duty. And you have already noted what the blessed Creator commanded the king, saying (Deuteronomy 17:17), "he shall not multiply wives for himself," and saying (ibid. 17:16), "only he shall not multiply horses for himself," and saying (cf. Nehemiah 13:26), "did not Solomon king of Israel sin because of these?" - despite all the strength of his intellect and the abundance of his understanding and greatness.

And he says further there, and strive to restrict the sense of taste, so that you take from food and drink only enough for your sustenance, and abstain from what is more than this. And the strategy for this matter is that you minimize the kinds of relish, and rely on one relish while you can, and likewise accustom your soul, at certain times, to be without relish, in order to train your belly and your nature, until the matter becomes easy for you when you refrain from it. And if you can forgo relish that involves labor and toil, and rely on what involves no labor at all, such as olives, figs, grapes, and the like, do so - and make your daytime eating lighter than your nighttime eating, if it is your custom to eat several times during the day, so that the movement of your limbs be light by day and the matters of your Torah and your worldly affairs be easy for you.

And afterward you shall practice fasting your body, if your body is strong, even one day a week, and everything you can accustom your soul to, not to feel concerning eating and drinking, in order to discipline it, do it, and make your intent in it more for healing than for nourishment - and let all your drinking be water, unless your intent with wine is to drink for the benefit of your body or to remove worry from your heart, as it is said (Proverbs 31:6), "give strong drink to the one who is perishing" - and be careful about excess of it and indulgence in it, and the gathering of people over it, for it is the great affliction for Torah and for the world - and the sage has already told of it what suffices (Proverbs 20:1), "wine is a scoffer, strong drink a brawler," and he says concerning food and drink (ibid. 23:20), "be not among winebibbers," and so on, "for the glutton and the drunkard shall come to poverty," and so on - to this point.

And this way the pious one, of blessed memory, wrote is the way of abstinence fitting for masters of Torah, whose main craft is Torah - for if a master of Torah wishes to rely on trust and spend his money eating meat or chickens and the like, kinds of pleasures, he is found troubling himself with the affairs of this world in pursuit of sustenance, and shall be idle from the words of Torah - and at a time he cannot find his custom, he shall not be able to bear it and shall fall ill. Therefore it is fitting for every Torah scholar to practice this abstinence that is written in Chovot HaLevavot.

And so there are several teachings of our Rabbis that support this and distance pleasures from masters of Torah - among them, first, the Baraita of "the acquisition of Torah" (Avot, chapter 6, mishnah 4-5): this is the way of Torah - you shall eat bread with salt, and so on - do not crave the table of kings. And our father Jacob, peace be upon him, asked only for "bread to eat and clothing to wear" (Genesis 28:20) - and through this the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, are fulfilled, who said (Parashat Terumah, page 141a), happy is he who derives no pleasure at all from its own [the husk]. And especially if he eats only for healing, as the pious one, of blessed memory, wrote, this is the more excellent aspect, that he derives no benefit at all from its own.

And so it is fitting for whoever wishes to sanctify himself that he eat only for healing, so that he not fall ill and be idle from Torah and commandments - therefore it is fitting that he not fill his soul with coarse foods, and even from good things he should not fully satisfy his desire, even on the Sabbath, for much eating causes much sleep, as they said, of blessed memory, in the first chapter of Yoma (mishnah, chapter 8 - actually referring to the High Priest before Yom Kippur), they would not feed him much, for food brings on sleep. And when he trains himself to content himself with a little, he shall find rest for his soul, and be sanctified in Torah, and shall not come to belch while studying.

And the wise person shall take this matter to heart, and abstain from his desire, and not fill his belly and his desire like a beast, for "who is mighty? He who subdues his inclination" (Avot, chapter 4, mishnah 1) - and if his inclination entices him to eat, he shall break his strength and subdue it from his desire, and then fear and holiness shall rest upon him, as it is written (Psalms 34:10), "fear the LORD, His holy ones."

And so the Ra'avad wrote in the Gate of Holiness, in these words: and I see that the great fence, the excellent guard, and the good path for subduing the inclination, is the hunger of the soul from minimizing its pleasures and delights in food and drink - except that he may enjoy a good aroma, and washing in hot water, since hot water is pleasant to him, and the little food he eats should be well seasoned and prepared, since it is pleasant to him, and his soul shall accept it and be content with a little of it - and he should always leave a little short of his full need and the completion of his desire, and shall not drink wine except well diluted, so that his mind not be confused by it. And along this path they said, of blessed memory (Gittin 70a), a meal from which you derive pleasure, withdraw your hand from it - and there are two great benefits in this matter: the first, that its eating not harm him, and the second, the subduing of the inclination and the breaking of desire. And just as we have said concerning a meal, so is the way for all the world's pleasures and delights, that a person not fill his full desire from them.

And needless to say that a person should guard himself from foods he knows to be harmful to him, for one who eats things harmful to him when he could avoid them is negligent of his body and negligent of his soul, because he follows his desire and does not care about the loss of his body - and this is the way of the evil inclination and its foolish counsel, to entice him from the way of life to the way of death. And every living, speaking being knows that the evil inclination has no way to him except through the way of the permitted, and the opening of its path is from what is permitted to him - and if he guards the opening, he needs no other guard.

And I have already set forth everything before you at the beginning of this Gate, that the way of that worthless counselor is to advise him to fill his desire from what is permitted to him, and after habituating him to filling his desire with what is permitted, and inducing his soul to be constantly eager and yearning for its pledge, it entices him toward the light prohibition, and from the light to the severe, as I have said. Therefore be careful with the permitted, and if you fence yourself with it and minimize your desire from what is permitted to you, you are assured that your inclination will no longer entice you toward the forbidden - for if a matter of prohibition arises, you immediately reason this a fortiori argument within yourself: if I was forbidden in what is permitted to me, how much more so in what is forbidden to me? And since you carry this a fortiori argument upon yourself, you are assured that you shall abstain from the lustful thought, and all the more so from the deed.

And a person should not afflict his soul [excessively], lest he weaken his heart and his deeds and his nature become corrupted, and his mind become confused, and his loss be greater than his gain, for he shall be idle from Torah and from prayer, and if he studies, his Torah shall not be settled, and he shall not agree properly on halachah and the dialectics of tradition, since Torah is acquired only through the essence of joy.

And a person should not withhold himself from any joy of a commandment or any pleasure of a commandment, only let his eyes be open against the inclination, and be careful that it not fill all his desires. And if he weakens his heart from eating too little, it is better for him to eat twice a day, little by little, and not fill his belly all at once - and if it is not convenient for him to eat twice a day, let him have among the confections that settle the heart, and eat a little of them, and his heart shall be strengthened. Also, if he sees in himself and by nature that he needs to fast a day or two, let him fast according to his condition, for one who sits in fasting when he needs it is called holy, provided he not be idle from Torah or from commandments because of it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:52-: Also, the oath, which is severe, was permitted to fence oneself at a time of transgression, as Boaz said concerning Ruth (Ruth 3:13), "as the LORD lives, lie down until morning" - our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Vayikra Rabbah 23:11), that his inclination accused him all night, saying to him, you are unmarried and she is unmarried, and a woman is acquired through intercourse - go and have relations with her and she shall be acquired to you through intercourse. Boaz leaped up and swore against the inclination, "as the LORD lives, lie down until morning" - he swore to the inclination that he would not do this, and to the woman, lie down until morning. So every person can know for himself the fence that would be good for him, whether subduing [his desire] or an oath. And I see that nothing is better than subduing and hunger of the soul, as I have said - and if he needs an oath as well, let him swear and fulfill it, along the lines of what David said (Psalms 119:106), "I have sworn, and I will fulfill it, to observe Your righteous judgments" - to this point.

And I, the youngest, say that this way is good for whoever it is possible for and has the means to acquire confections, but whoever is poor and lacks the means to conduct himself this way should at least conduct his eating according to what is needed for health, as Rambam wrote in Hilchot De'ot (chapter 4), in what he wrote, that a person should minimize his eating, for this is the correct way. Especially one who does not fast - it is good that he minimize his morning meal so that he not be idle from the occupation with Torah, and he should gauge in his mind that his measure of eating be in two sessions, morning and evening, equal to the measure of what he was accustomed to being satisfied by at one time.

And for whoever wishes to be constant in rising at midnight to occupy himself with Torah, let him put his main eating in the morning meal, and at night eat only fruits - and let them be dried fruits, such as raisins, almonds, walnuts, and figs. And let him distance himself at night from eating coarse foods, such as cheese and the like, but rather conduct himself as the Ra'avad wrote above, at the beginning of his words, that he eat a little, well seasoned and prepared, and the bread be less than the cooked dish - and for whoever wishes to read most of the night, it is good that he not eat bread at all at night. And so my teacher, peace be upon him, was accustomed, when he was not fasting. And a penitent accustomed to fasting every day, on days when he shall eat, such as Rosh Chodesh and festivals, should conduct himself along this way we have written.

And for whoever the way the Ra'avad, peace be upon him, wrote is possible, as a repair for the day, it is good as a repair for the night, that he eat at night only kinds of confections that settle the heart - and through this he can withstand most of the night in the occupation with Torah without sleep - and it is found that through this he bears some affliction, and does not pursue pleasures, for Torah endures only in one who distances himself from pleasure, as they said in the Zohar (Parashat Pinchas, page 247a), on the verse (cf. Numbers 28:5), "fine flour mixed with beaten oil" - it is explained there that "fine flour" is the Shechinah; "mixed with oil," it says of it, this is the oil that flows and goes forth from above. And it says afterward, the Ra'aya Meheimna said, holy lamp, how sweet are your words - certainly it is said here, "mixed with beaten oil," and it is said there concerning the Oral Torah, "mixed" with Scripture, with Mishnah, and with Talmud, and so on. And there is a second secret: "mixed with beaten oil" - certainly Torah is not "mixed" except for one who endures several poundings for its sake, as the masters of the Mishnah established, that Torah endures only in one who kills himself over it. And it says further, at the time you pound your feet from country to country, you shall merit to see the countenance of the Shechinah. And further, "mixed with beaten oil" - this is one who fulfills "you shall eat bread with salt, and drink water by measure." And further, "mixed with beaten oil" - this is what is written (Isaiah 53:5), "and he was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities" - to this point.

Behold, it is explicit that the Torah, called "fine flour," endures in a person only if he pounds himself and kills himself and fulfills "you shall eat bread with salt." And although it says "and further" [several times], all these explanations come to one place - that the intent is the pounding of matter so that the Torah and the soul shine within it, and this is the way to attain Torah - that even if he is wealthy, he should not practice indulgences for himself - and this is what it says (Avot, chapter 6, mishnah 4), "this is the way of Torah," and so on. And this is what King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 119:71), "it is good for me that I was afflicted, so that I might learn Your statutes."

And it says in the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit, page 11a) that Rashbi, peace be upon him, and Rabbi Elazar, when they came out of the cave, and Rabbi Pinchas went to see him - they said, of blessed memory: he went to him and found him with a changed appearance, his body full of cracks [sores]. He wept with him and said, woe, that I see you thus. He said, happy is my portion that you see me thus, for had you not seen me thus, I would not be thus - to this point. And so they said in the Talmud, Tractate Shabbat (33b). Behold, it is explicit that through the sufferings he endured in the cave, he attained wondrous wisdom - and so they said in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu, that in the thirteen years Rashbi, peace be upon him, was confined in the cave, the depths of wisdom were revealed to him and he attained knowledge of future things.

And especially one who has sins must endure sufferings for his sins and shall not merit the supernal light, which is the oil concerning which David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 23:5), "You anoint my head with oil" - unless he pounds himself. And this is what it says, "and further, 'mixed with beaten oil' - this is what is written, 'and he was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities'" - and the intent is that just as the Messiah suffers, our iniquities cause him to be crushed - if so, whoever wishes that the Messiah not be crushed by our iniquities should himself suffer and be crushed. And so it is explained in Sefer Chasidim (siman 528), that a certain pious man endured several sufferings for his sins and gave this reason mentioned - see there.

Further, in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu, brought in the Yalkut, Parashat Va'etchanan (siman 830, page 265, col. 3), on the verse "I am the LORD your God," in these words: a person who does not merit that the Torah enter into his bowels should seek mercy concerning excessive eating and drinking, that it not enter his bowels, as it is said (Isaiah 48:10), "I have refined you, but not with silver; I have tested you in the furnace of affliction" - just as this furnace, even if you put into it all the wood in the world, burns and destroys it, so a person's throat, even if you give it all the foods in the world, destroys them - to this point.

Further, they said in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 19:1): Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said, words of Torah require blackening and evening [dedication morning and evening] - and where do we know of sustenance? "Who provides for the raven its prey" (Job 38:41) - so, unless a person becomes cruel toward his own body, his children, and his household, like this raven, he does not merit the words of Torah - to this point.

And the reason the Torah does not rest upon a person except after he distances pleasures from himself is because the Torah is called holy, as it is said (Proverbs 2:5), "and you shall find the knowledge of God" - and therefore it rests only in a place where there is holiness and abstinence from bodily pleasures.

And Rabbi Yisrael, of blessed memory, wrote in Sefer Menorat HaMaor: great is the Torah, whose holiness is such that even from bread and water Moses needed to sanctify himself before receiving the Torah, as it is said (Exodus 34:28), "and he was there with the LORD" [forty days and forty nights, without bread or water] - and is this not an a fortiori argument? If from bread and water, which are pure, he needed to sanctify himself for forty days, how much more so should we sanctify ourselves for the words of Torah from all impurity - to this point.

And what appears to me concerning the intent of eating, according to what is understood from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, is what is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, page 154b), that there is a supernal table upon which is the showbread - and it says, and from the secret of this table, sustenance goes out to the world, according to what is given into it from above, and that bread is the fruit and sustenance that goes out from this table, to show that from this table fruits, produce, and sustenance go out to the world - if there were no vineyard, the grapes that are its fruit, going out from it, would not be found; if there were no tree, its fruit would not be found in the world - therefore the table is the essential thing, and the sustenance that goes out from it is that bread.
